primary_meaning: Christ as the rejected yet chosen cornerstone—the secure foundation of salvation, faith, and the people of God.
primary_basis: Psalm 118:22: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone.
Isaiah 28:16: God lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone as a sure foundation.
Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10–11; Luke 20:17: Jesus applies the rejected-stone text to himself.
Acts 4:11–12: Jesus is the rejected stone who became the cornerstone, with salvation found in him.
Romans 9:32–33: Christ is both the stone over which unbelievers stumble and the one in whom believers trust.
1 Peter 2:4–8: Christ is the living, chosen cornerstone; he is also a stone of stumbling to the disobedient.
Ephesians 2:20–22: Christ is the cornerstone of the spiritual temple formed by God's people.

alternatives.meaning: God or Christ as rock-like strength, protection, permanence, and refuge.
Believers collectively as “living stones” built into the Church or spiritual temple.
Spiritual hardness, insensibility, or resistance to God, especially in the expression “heart of stone.”
An obstacle of stumbling, offense, judgment, or ruin for those who reject God or Christ.
The divinely established kingdom that destroys worldly kingdoms and fills the earth, represented by Daniel's stone; some Christian traditions identify the stone more directly with Christ.
A memorial, witness, or enduring testimony to God's acts and covenant commitments.
The permanence and authority of divine law, associated with commandments written on stone tablets.
A new identity, acquittal, victory, or admission to the messianic banquet, symbolized by the white stone in Revelation; the exact background is disputed.

notes: “Stone” is highly context-dependent and has no single settled symbolic meaning across Scripture. The dominant specifically Christian use is christological—Jesus as the rejected stone and cornerstone—but hardness, refuge, stumbling, the Church, memorial testimony, and God's kingdom are also established readings.
